The metaverse is swiftly ﬂattering an important player in the e-commerce domain. It provides innumerable opportunities and
indicates a revolutionary paradigm shift in e-commerce. Online businesses can now create virtual storefronts that enable
immersive, lifelike product exploration within the metaverse, in contrast to traditional brick-and-mortar stores that cater to
local customers. Current research oﬀers a novel conceptual framework based on theories of interactive media eﬀects and the
stimulus–organism–response paradigm to understand consumer purchase intentions in the metaverse. Carefully gathered data
from 342 survey participants were then examined using the analytical tools of structural equation modelling (SEM) and
importance–performance map analysis (IPMA). The results of the study shed light on how much perceived augmentation and
interaction aﬀect consumers’ cognitive and emotive reactions, including feelings of realism, immersion, and telepresence.
Remarkably, these reactions have a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on how customers behave. The study’s distinctive worth is found in its
creative recommendations, which can help tech ﬁrms and metaverse developers improve the purchasing experience in this
dynamic digital environment.
Keywords: augmentation; immersion; interactivity; metaverse; realism; telepresence; virtual commerce
1. Introduction
Metaverse is an envisioned world with continually increas-
ing immersive digital spaces that provide a highly interac-
tive environment for various business sectors [1]. It is an
extension of synchronous communication that enables
users to share the immersive experience with other mem-
bers of the group. The newest trend in digital engagement
is the metaverse immersive experience. These immersive
experiences will incorporate metaverses—wealthy, diligent,
shared intuitively confronts with collaboration and co-crea-
tion, as well as complete working shared economies—beside
other experiences focused on shopping, work preparing,
play and gaming, instruction, massive cultural gatherings,
etc., [2]. The metaverse concept enables human interaction
and communication over the internet [3]. Metaverse is deﬁned
as follows:
“A persistent and immersive simulated world
that is experienced in the ﬁrst person by large
groups of simultaneous users who share a strong
sense of mutual presence” (Loius [4]).

Regardless of the fact that the metaverse is still in its
infancy, many well-known and proﬁtable brands have
already made signiﬁcant investments in its development
[5]. The metaverse has intriguing prospects because it can
seamlessly combine our actual and virtual lives into a fully
immersive experience [6]. Although it may be a leap of faith
to anticipate that the metaverse will entirely replace our
regular communication within the next ﬁve 5, it is unques-
tionably set to play a signiﬁcant role in millions of users’
daily engagements. It provides numerous opportunities to
brands [7].
The metaverse has the power to aﬀect customers’ feel-
ings, thoughts, and behavior signiﬁcantly. Metaverse set-
tings expand the capabilities of conventional web-based
e-commerce by enabling face-to-face encounters and close
involvement with items [3]. They achieve this by incorpo-
rating operational and interactive aspects. Metaverse enables
businesses to create online shops where customers can try
on clothing using avatars that are like them. Customers
may now interact with products virtually through the utili-
zation of virtual reality technology and ﬁll the gap left by
a lack of in-person interaction [8]. By simulating real-
world interactions in a mediated setting, the metaverse is
anticipated to create a potent feeling of immersion. Cus-
tomers’ perceptions will undoubtedly improve as a result
of their increased immersion in the activity and attachment
to the products [9].
However, recently, many retailers have adopted immer-
sive technology capabilities to their e-commerce websites
as well as integrated their mobile applications that allow
users to try products before purchasing [10]. Shoppers can
stay at home and explore virtual stores longer than tradi-
tional online stores if they are more vivid and immersive
[11]. The idea of trying before you buy helps the customers
to alleviate the risk associated with a lack of product contact
and involvement [12, 13]. Leading companies including Self-
ridges, Charli Cohen, and Pokémon have created a fashion
centric metaverse hub where people can explore and buy vir-
tual clothing for their avatars [14]. Similarly, ZARA and
Adidas have opened virtual stores by oﬀering an opportunity
to buy digital goods that can be delivered to customers phys-
ically [15]. Smart devices and metaverse technology reduce
consumer hesitations and uncertainties in online shopping
by enhancing the overall buying experience [16, 17].
In virtual reality studies, telepresence is found to be an
essential factor because it simulates real-world cognitive
and sensory inputs, which aﬀects how consumers perceive
products and services [12, 18]. Nevertheless, despite these
predicted advantages, empirical research into consumers’
immersive experiences and perceptions of being present in
the metaverse is still lacking.
This study delves into the metaverse’s transformative
potential and oﬀers a comprehensive conceptual framework
to understand consumers’ purchase intentions within this
emerging digital realm. Grounded in theories of interactive
media eﬀects and the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R)
paradigm, we explore how the metaverse inﬂuences con-
sumers’ cognitive and emotional responses, ultimately
shaping their behavioral outcomes. The interaction of aug-
mentation and interactivity in customers’ virtual buying
experiences was examined by Sundar et al. [19], using the
theory of interactive media eﬀects (TIME). According to
the TIME, the characteristics of the metaverse may work
as a catalyst for consumers to experience psychological
changes, become fully engaged in the media, and then
reveal behavioral reactions [17, 19]. In a nutshell, psycho-
logical links are predictions that help to understand how
technology aﬀects consumers and how consumers interact
with the technology. These correlates are formed from dis-
tinctive media traits or attributes [20].
This study is one of the primary research projects that
looked into the relationship between consumers’ attitudes
and behaviors when engaging with metaverse stores and
their perception of being fully engaged and absorbed. In
light of this research gap, we have extended the TIME model
to align with the speciﬁc context of our study. Our novel
framework provides a critical insight into the aspects that
compel end-users to exhibit behavioral responses in the
metaverse. Within this framework, we identify consumers’
perceived augmentation and interactivity as pivotal elements
that give rise to a profound sense of telepresence when users
engage with the metaverse. This sense of telepresence, in
turn, serves as an intermediary variable, elucidating the
mechanisms behind metaverse consumers’ experiences of
immersion and realism. Our research focuses on two distinct
dimensions of behavioral response: consumers’ attitudes
toward reusing the metaverse and their purchase intentions
within this digital realm. The theoretical groundwork of
our study is rooted in the well-established S-O-R framework
and the TIME. We hope to increase knowledge in this grow-
ing subject by advancing the understanding of the complex
relationships between customers’ attitudes, experiences,
and subsequent behaviors in the metaverse by modifying
and applying these theoretical frameworks to the metaverse
setting.
This research study’s remaining sections are organized
subsequently: the initial section is an introduction, and the
subsequent section presents the theoretical background of
the framework. In the third part, hypotheses were developed
after a thorough understanding of consumers’ behaviors and
experiences in the metaverse shopping malls. The fourth sec-
tion illustrates the methods and techniques whereas the ﬁfth
section talks about results and ﬁndings. Finally, the last sec-
tion wraps up the discussion of the ramiﬁcations based on
our results and provides some suggestions for future
research. The list of acronyms used in this study are pro-
vided in Appendix A.
2. Background and Theoretical Framework
2.1. Metaverse. In recent times, the scientiﬁc network has
paid considerable attention to the idea of the metaverse in
e-commerce. The term “metaverse” refers to a virtual real-
ity–based digital cosmos where users can engage in immer-
sive and lifelike interactions with one another and their
surroundings. This cutting-edge technology can completely
transform how users interact with e-commerce platforms
by providing distinctive and improved buying experiences.

With the emergence of the metaverse, the internet has chan-
ged and now allows users to navigate complex 3D virtual
worlds in real time [21]. Reliable information is provided
in this immersive environment in a variety of ﬁelds, such
as e-commerce, tourism, education, and healthcare [22].
Numerous business opportunities have been generated by
the metaverse. These consist of businesses that use virtual
music events, nonfungible tokens (NFTs), and more readily
accessible product information [6]. The metaverse addresses
present constraints, like the lack of in-person engagement
and instantaneous product connection, to enhance user
functioning and involvement in electronic commerce [8].
The retail industry is changing due to the metaverse, which
presents both unprecedented challenges and opportunities
for companies to interact with their clients in novel and
inventive ways. In the metaverse, companies can create 3D
virtual stores where shoppers can try on products using digital
versions of themselves [23]. In order to increase understanding
and improve the metaverse shopping experience, consumers
can create realistic digital representations of themselves using
tools like Unreal Engine’s MetaHuman Creator. Unlike tradi-
tional online shopping, which requires users to spend hours
browsing websites, reading reviews, and watching commer-
cials, purchasing in the metaverse seamlessly combines the
actual world and the virtual one [24].
2.2. Conceptual Framework
2.2.1. S-O-R Framework. According to the S-O-R frame-
work, it is established that the external environment has a
substantial impact on people’s cognitive and emotional
states, which in turn causes them to exhibit particular behav-
ioral reactions [25]. The S-O-R paradigm meticulously
examines the intricate dynamics among three fundamental
components: stimulus, organisms, and responses [26]. The
architectural characteristics of an internet-based system
and the collective set of its functionalities can be described
as the stimulus in the context of the metaverse environment
because both have a direct inﬂuence on the internal psycho-
logical states of users. The stimulus component basically acts
as the catalyst for an inducer of individual reactions. This
study considers the characteristics (perceived augmentation
and interactivity) as the metaverse stimuli. The organism
component of the S-O-R architecture is supported by the
cognitive and aﬀective auxiliary state of the users, which
reveals the mediating processes that occur between the stim-
uli and consumers’ responses [27]. Consumers’ mental pro-
cesses are represented by their cognitive state, which is made
up of “everything that happens through the consumers’
thoughts regarding the acquisition, processing, retention,
and retrieving of information” [28]. Consumers’ reactions
to environmental stimuli, such as arousal and pleasure, are
reﬂected in their aﬀective states [29]. Once exposed to the
stimuli, consumers translate the stimuli into important
information that is useful to them in decision-making. Since
perception and aﬀection are fundamental dimensions of the
shopper experience, this study posits that consumers’ sense
of presence, immersion, and realism (an organism state) in
the metaverse will be inspired by the eﬀects of surrounding
clues (stimuli). The S-O-R framework has been applied to
a spectrum of ﬁelds such as computer experience [29], social
media advertising [30], virtual reality studies [31], and many
other related areas. This study explores users’ conative
behavioral responses in metaverse retail malls because the
response might also be attitudinal.
2.2.2. The TIME. According to the TIME, technological attri-
butes of digital media manipulate human behaviors due to
the immersive experiences of users [19]. Aﬀordance is a core
element of the TIME that makes possible any system or
application useable by its users. Usually, it is linked with
emotional associations of users such as perceived realism,
the experience of telepresence, and immersion [32]. The
metaverse’s content can be tailored to the user’s body
dimensions to increase the sense of immersion and realism
[17]. The type of users’ interactions with a system can be
determined by cognitive associations derived from aﬀor-
dances if the media features are clear and correctly convey
the basic aﬀordances to its users [19]. Whereas robust psy-
chological links of consumers’ behavior may have an impact
on those responses, it is important to recognize that cus-
tomers’
immersive
experiences—such
as
telepresence,
immersion, and realism—play a substantial mediating func-
tion [17]. According to past research, aﬀordance-driven
engagement, such as telepresence, immersion, and realism,
serves as the intermediary among cognitive, aﬀective, and
conative reactions [33]. Studies have employed TIME to
analyze how distinct media qualities can be transferred into
consumers’ reactions since they have recognized its capacity
to reclassify major media attributes simply in terms of non-
message characteristics [34]. As an illustration, Donghee
[35] argued that psychological associations generated by
consumers’ interaction might be transformed into immer-
sive experiences, which could be able to cause subsequent
aﬀective, cognitive, and conative responses toward virtual
applications. Figure 1 illustrates our conceptual model.
3. Hypothesis Development
3.1. Media Characteristics (Aﬀordances) or Stimulus Factors.
Media characteristics act as a facilitator among consumers’
technology interactions and responses [36]. Each medium
has its distinct media qualities, technological framework,
and interactive elements [17]. TIME theorized that media
qualities are aﬀordances that are provided to consumers
who internally analyze pertinent and prominent features
and experience medium attributes through their views,
which lead to consumers’ immersion [19, 37]. A communi-
cation medium’s aﬀordance serves as the foundation for a
TIME. This is often considered an interface characteristic
that may be attributed to the technology of the medium
rather than the communication source or content. Accord-
ing to traditional deﬁnitions, “aﬀordance is a medium where
users meet” [38, 39]. This interaction is aﬀordance-driven
and modiﬁes how users’ knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors
are impacted by media content. Prior studies support the
idea that media components inﬂuence consumers’ immer-
sive experiences in the context of the TIME [32, 35, 40]. In

3.1.1. Perceived Augmentation. The term “augmentation”
refers to the enrichment of the surroundings where the vir-
tual and physical parts are no longer diﬀerentiated from
one another due to virtual technology [41]. The virtual space
can be augmented with text, geolocation data, music, and
visual elements like pictures or videos on a variety of levels
[40]. According to various studies [28, 42], augmentation
can aﬀect consumer responses in addition to other signiﬁ-
cant media properties like telepresence, vividness, and inter-
activity. Furthermore, users’ perceived augmentation has a
signiﬁcant impact on many aspects of human communica-
tion including perceived telepresence and persuasiveness
[43]. For instance, while watching a movie, viewers could
have the impression that they are inside a certain scene, or
when shopping online, customers might get the impression
that they are in a physical store. Interaction in the virtual
environment is linked to users’ ability to modify the content
and structure of a mediated environment in real time [44,
45]. Similar to an AR-based virtual world, augmentation is
a distinctive and salient feature for metaverse retailers [33,
41]. Perceived augmentation in metaverse contexts provides
a new level of media characteristics due to its speciﬁcally
observable technology. In comparison to conventional VR-
based technology, the augmentation characteristics of meta-
verse technology enable more para-authentic product expe-
riences, which has the potential to enhance consumers’
immersive experiences [46]. Similarly Javornik et al. [40]
indicated that perceived augmentation has a signiﬁcant pos-
itive inﬂuence on immersive experiences. Given the discus-
sion above, the following can be hypothesized.
Hypothesis 1. Consumers’ perceived augmentation positively
aﬀects telepresence in the metaverse stores.
3.1.2. Perceived Interactivity. Consumers’ interactions with
virtual goods might be facilitated or hindered by technical
traits in an immersive virtual world. The avatars’ actions
serve as a channel for the communication within the meta-
verse environment [9]. The level of user interaction with vir-
tual objects and the ability to instantly adapt to the content
of a mediated environment is known as interactivity [45].
The level of interactivity of a medium depends on its techno-
logical underpinnings, for example, system reaction times,
user control over virtual worlds, and methods for studying
user behavior in the metaverse. Interactivity in online shop-
ping channels has been found to foster the emotional
response of retailers’ attitudes [47], shopping participation
[48], purchase intention, and satisfaction [12]. The user’s
avatar adjusts himself to the virtual world environment
because of self-control in the virtual environment provided
by interactivity [49]. Thus, the interactivity aﬀected by ava-
tars distorts users’ sense of reality by transferring them to
the virtual world and creating a sense of telepresence [50].
According to the TIME, these are user-presented fundamen-
tal aﬀordances that have the potential to be tied to psycho-
logical
correlates
including
control,
connectivity,
and
responsiveness [40]. Customers frequently view interactivity
as a key feature of the metaverse since it allows them to alter
the stimuli and use telepresence to share their interactions
with others [51]. For instance, virtual shopping gives cus-
tomers the chance to broaden their connection with a variety
of goods, such as virtual clothing, jewelry, and properties,
which makes it easier for them to realize their ideal selves
[52]. If consumers believe that the avatar is an extension of
themselves, the investments in self-identity development will
be more enjoyable and engaging. Such fascinating participa-
tion in metaverse exchanges and explorations lowers self-
consciousness, thereby making the virtual experience more
enjoyable while improving ﬂow and immersive experience
[53, 54]. Thus, this study proposes the following.
Hypothesis 2. Consumers’ interactivity positively aﬀects tele-
presence in the metaverse stores.

3.2. Organismic and Mediating Factors (O)
3.2.1. Telepresence. In contrast to actual surrounds, “tele-
presence,” as deﬁned by Steuer [45], measures a person’s
sensation of being within a virtual environment. The word
was ﬁrst used by Shih [55], to explain how viewers of sports
media could feel as though they were in the room. The
degree of telepresence is mostly determined by human sen-
sory engagement, which is contingent upon the media
device’s ability to replicate visual data with a high degree
of ﬁdelity, regardless of the format. As Shin and Han [56]
pointed out, immersive, information-rich virtual reality
settings have profoundly altered user perceptions and pro-
duced an incredibly captivating whole experience. A num-
ber of studies have conﬁrmed that people who have
experienced telepresence are less likely to notice signiﬁcant
diﬀerences between real and virtual environments [9, 57,
58]. Telepresence can lead to a greater level of perceived
realism with the simulated environment and a sense of
immersion as their peripheral reality [59]. Researchers have
previously hypothesized that telepresence has a favorable
eﬀect on shoppers’ attitudes and behaviors [60]. Telepre-
sence aﬀects users’ attitudes and behavioral intentions,
which can lead to positive cognitive and aﬀective assess-
ments in the virtual environment [61]. Immersive experi-
ences enable the user to engage with an environment that
oﬀers a constant ﬂow of inputs and experiences [62, 63].
Immersive experiences vary by individual and are created
by a person’s processing of sensory data from their sur-
roundings [64]. Similarly, McLean and Wilson [20] asserted
that telepresence can improve users’ perceptions of realism
and beneﬁt users by fostering and strengthening a favorable
attitude toward virtual worlds. Therefore, telepresence
increases consumers’ sense of immersion and realism,
which will ultimately result in a positive attitude toward
reuse and purchase in the metaverse. Hence, we propose
the following.
Hypothesis 3a. Telepresence positively aﬀects consumers’
sense of immersion in the metaverse stores.
Hypothesis 3b. Telepresence positively aﬀects consumers’
realism in the metaverse stores.
3.2.2. Sense of Immersion. A sense of immersion is deﬁned
as an “individual’s psychological reaction to the mediated
environments” [65]. There are two types of immersion,
namely, user-focused and system-focused immersion. The
ability of the technology to create a compelling and immer-
sive environment that the user can engage with is referred
to as sensory immersion or system-focused [66]. Sekhavat
and Zarei [67] described user-focused immersion as “a psy-
chological condition deﬁned by experiencing oneself to be
immersed by, involved in, and engaging with an environ-
ment that produces a constant stream of inputs and sensa-
tions” (i.e., metaverse stores). A suﬃcient number of
immersive features must be included in the system to facil-
itate an immersive environment that elicits consumer reac-
tions to products [65]. Scholars contend that the mediated
environment that fosters a stronger sensation of immersion
will result in greater levels of presence [63]. AR-based apps
can successfully immerse consumers and deliver the sense
that virtual objects are physically present in their physical
surrounding, which enable the consumers to assess prod-
ucts virtually [46]. Immersion creates an impression of vir-
tual objects as existing in the real world, highlighting the
connection between immersion and product presence
[68]. This study employs a user-focused approach and con-
siders immersion as a psychological condition because the
technology part of immersion is addressed by the augmen-
tation powers provided by the metaverse. This study is
interested in understanding how media characteristics
aﬀect consumer immersion in metaverse shopping malls
and relevant conative responses. The following hypotheses
are put forth.
Hypothesis 4a. Consumer’s sense of immersion will positively
aﬀect attitude to reuse of metaverse.
Hypothesis 4b. Consumer’s sense of immersion will positively
aﬀect purchase intentions in metaverse.
3.2.3. Perceived Realism Experience. Realism is deﬁned as
“the audience’s assessment of how closely the ﬁctional uni-
verse resembles the real world” [69]. Four technology
dimensions—sensory, interaction, control, and location—-
work together to improve VR experiences by enhancing
the impression of reality or presence [70]. These four dimen-
sions play a very important role in reproducing more realis-
tic virtual settings. Realism has two subdimensions, that is,
“social realism and perceptual realism” [69]. Social realism
is deﬁned as a “realistic or believable illustration of the phys-
ical world, which portrays things that occurred or could hap-
pen in the actual world”. On the other hand, perceptual
realism “realistically creates the physical world by oﬀering
rich sensory stimuli” [71]. As a result, the concept of per-
ceived realism refers to how realistic a virtual experience is
about the surroundings of virtual settings and how this has
improved the consumer’s actions [71–73]. The studies of
realism have observed positive eﬀects on provocation, pres-
ence, and enjoyment [74, 75]. Hust et al. [76] stated that per-
ceived realism and interactions play a signiﬁcant role in the
students’ information gathering. Virtual worlds have been
designed to create an immersive and engaging experience.
Ivory and Kalyanaraman [77] describe that higher levels of
realism in video games or avatars do not have adverse con-
sequences on players’ emotions, presence, or behavior.
Therefore, if a consumer experiences the product’s presence
in their actual environment, the more metaverse interactions
will be regarded as “real.” Therefore, we propose the follow-
ing hypothesis.
Hypothesis 5a. Perceived realism is positively related to atti-
tude to reuse of metaverse.
Hypothesis 5b. Perceived realism is positively related to pur-
chase intentions in metaverse.

3.3. Conative Response (R)
3.3.1. Attitude to Reuse of Metaverse. The overall attitude
toward a behavior has been deﬁned as a user’s “positive or
negative feelings” about engaging in a speciﬁc behavior
[78]. The feeling connected to using the metaverse is refer-
enced in this work by consumers’ conative behavior toward
their intentions to shop in the metaverse stores. The idea of
presence, according to Mollen and Wilson [79] may support
another experience construct that in turn may evoke con-
sumer attitudes. We anticipate that consumers’ perceptions
of immersion and realism may play a mediating role in
motivating their behavioral reaction to the metaverse. Cus-
tomers may try on products and assess the ﬁt of the products
in a virtual environment due to the level of immersion cre-
ated by the augmented environment [65, 80]. The evidence
from the technology acceptance model and Ajzen’s theory
of planned behavior supports the concept that attitudes
toward technology inﬂuence a user’s intention to use it
[81]. Accordingly, Park and Yoo [82] demonstrated that
consumers develop positive behavioral intentions after pur-
chasing cosmetic products via AR-based web apps. Similar
ﬁndings were obtained in the marketing and retailing envi-
ronment by Pantano, Rese, and Baier [83] that augmented
environments aﬀect consumers’ behavior intentions and
purchasing intentions positively. The diﬀerent levels of
cognitive processing inﬂuence consumers’ attitudes about
objects; they engage in their buying activities and these feel-
ings inﬂuence their intentions for action [84]. Accordingly,
one’s intention to revisit metaverse stores is more likely if
they have a positive feeling about them. In other words, con-
sumers’ feelings of immersion and realism in the metaverse
help consumers to revisit the metaverse stores in the future.
The conclusion derived from the literature suggests that
technologically and socially improved experiences increase
customers’ sense of telepresence, immersion, and realism
as well as their propensity to make purchases [85].
Hypothesis 6. Attitude to reuse of metaverse of metaverse
stores is positively related to purchase intentions in metaverse.
4. Methods
4.1. Sample and Data Collection Procedure. This study
adopted the survey questionnaire approach because it has
been regularly used for the study related to social commerce
behaviors [86]. Furthermore, the model employed in this
study is comprehensive and incorporates characteristics of
social interaction that are diﬃcult to quantify using other
methods. For the current study, we chose a survey approach
for this study as it is well suited to investigate social com-
merce behaviors [87]. Therefore, we recruited participants
through Telegram (https://t.me/Metaverse_Blockchain) for
data collection. Registered members of Telegram channels
and social media group admins helped distribute the online
questionnaire to potential users via email and WhatsApp.
We chose Telegram as the platform for data collection due
to its vibrant and diverse communities. These community
groups have thousands of daily active users who play virtual
games, publish blogs, communicate, seek help, and share
new ideas with other metaverse community members. We
briefed the study respondents before starting the question-
naire. We asked them some simple questions; for example,
do you frequently visit metaverse platforms Sandbox,
Roblox, Decentraland, etc.? Have you recently visited any
metaverse shopping malls, such as H&M, ZARA, Adidas,
and Gucci? With the support of registered members of tele-
gram channels and admins of social media groups, the
online questionnaire was provided to potential users via
email and WhatsApp. The data collection strategy has
followed the rule of thumb, that is, 10 to 20 times as many
cases as variables included in the study. We distributed 375
questionnaires and received 357 responses. We further elim-
inated 15 incomplete surveys of respondents who did not
have metaverse experience or knowledge. For the ﬁnal data
analysis, 342 valid responses were attained.
4.2. Measures and Data Analysis. The measurement items
adapted from previous research were pretested by experi-
enced individuals. The pretest evaluated their logical consis-
tency, readability, and contextual relevance. Feedback from
experts and respondents, particularly on the survey’s length,
language, and instructions, was carefully incorporated to
reﬁne the survey design and ensure clarity and eﬀectiveness.
This survey has two sections: the ﬁrst collects general
demographic information (gender, age, education level,
and frequency of metaverse usage), while the second part
covers the seven research constructs. Five telepresence and
purchase intention measurement items were modiﬁed for
use in metaverse scenarios and were adapted from Lin
et al. [50]. In contrast, the items for sense of immersion were
adapted from Fornerino, Helme-Guizon, and Gotteland
[88]. At the same time, the items for perceived augmentation
and interactivity were taken from Javornik [17] and Daeh-
wan and Yong [89], respectively. The metaverse reuses atti-
tude item, and perceived realism items were modiﬁed from
Daassi and Debbabi [65]. Appendix B contains all measuring
items and their sources. Responses have been recorded on a
ﬁve-point Likert scale (1 being strongly disagree, and 5 being
strongly agree). In order to examine complicated mediation
theories with a variety of indicators and interactions, this
study used partial least squares structural equation model-

6. Discussion and Implications
6.1. Discussion of Findings. This study explores how per-
ceived augmentation and interactivity
aﬀect customer
conative behaviors (particularly attitude and purchase
intention) in the context of metaverse technology. It is
based on the TIME and S-O-R paradigms. According to
our preliminary research, metaverse technology oﬀers users
a wider range of augmentation and interaction options
than traditional two-dimensional media. Furthermore, the
telepresence is markedly improved by these two dimen-
sions. This is consistent with the basic premise of telepre-
sence theory, which holds that heightened vividness and
interactive features are the cause of telepresence [45]. Stud-
ies on telepresence in relation to virtual reality technology
also supported this hypothesis [9, 50]. In the following
investigation, we examined the impact that users’ organis-
mic experiences in the metaverse have on their conative
behavior.
Three organismic criteria were included in our study:
perceived realism, sense of immersion, and telepresence.
First, as noted by Debbabi, Daassi, and Baile [97], telepre-
sence has a signiﬁcant and favorable impact on perceived
realism and immersion, which in turns shapes consumers’
conative behavioral responses. Second, in the metaverse,
customers’ intentions to make purchases are positively and
signiﬁcantly impacted by their sense of immersion. How-
ever, it does not have a substantial eﬀect on how customers
feel about reusing the metaverse.
In the ﬁeld of virtual retailing, our results are consistent
with previous studies conducted by Deng, Unnava, and Lee
[98]; Dwivedi et al. [99]; Laukkanen et al. [100]; Liu et al.
[101]; and Nikhashemi et al. [41]. Notably, we found that
consumers’ perceptions of realism had a favorable and sig-
niﬁcant inﬂuence on their propensity to reuse metaverse
stores as well as their buy intents [37, 65, 102]. All of our

6.3. Practical Implications. The study’s ﬁndings have
important ramiﬁcations for investors, developers, and
metaverse platform ﬁrms who have a stake in knowing
how customers plan to purchase in the metaverse. Notably,
metaverse augmentations and interactions enhance con-
sumers’ feelings of telepresence, enhancing their total
response. Nonetheless, considering how metaverse retail is
still developing, it is a relevant advice for metaverse
designers to concentrate on creating and modifying user
interfaces that enhance telepresence and enhance immer-
sion and realism. Improving user control and oﬀering a
more realistic and immersive experience are the best way
to improve metaverse retail businesses’ user interfaces
[60]. Furthermore, our research supports a thorough com-
prehension of how the organismic experience is formed in
the setting of metaverse retail. Based on strong and sophis-
ticated media qualities, the telepresence experience can trig-
ger cognitive, aﬀective, and behavioral reactions that are
mostly mediated by users’ direct interactions [97]. In addi-
tion, metaverse service providers ought to give equal weight
to improving the ﬁdelity between avatars and customers’
representations. This can be achieved by incorporating
metaverse technologies into their retail locations rather
than focusing only on improving the ﬁdelity between ava-
tars and customers’ representations through sophisticated
3D simulation techniques.
The study ﬁndings suggest that metaverse developers
should prioritize technology and its impact on user experi-
ences. Metaverse companies can boost engagement by
enabling dynamic, immersive customer interactions. More-
over, as our inquiry has shed light on, clients receive more
engaging experiences when they perceive realism, which is
why it is a crucial factor in guaranteeing the attractiveness
of metaverse retail businesses. Businesses operating in the
metaverse commerce space must provide users with the
most realistic augmented environments possible, closely rep-
licating how users interact with real-world objects. Busi-
nesses can improve customer perceptions in metaverse
shopping environments through immersive, lifelike, and
interactive features that strengthen telepresence. This study
particularly focuses on consumer attitudes and purchase
intentions, as opposed to a comprehensive investigation of
every marketing component. Besides, as this study has
shown, the sense of realism provides consumers with
enhanced and engaging experiences, which is a crucial factor
in guaranteeing the attractiveness of metaverse retail busi-
nesses. For companies operating in the metaverse commerce
space, providing clients with the most realistic augmented
surroundings that closely mimic their interactions with
physical products in real life is essential. Businesses can
improve their customer perceptions in metaverse shopping
environments by strengthening telepresence with immer-
sive, lifelike, and interactive features.
6.4. Limitations and Future Research Avenue. To summarize,
our research has provided valuable insights; yet, it is imper-
ative to recognize a number of fascinating directions for
future investigation. First oﬀ, there is no denying that
researchers are still drawn to investigating methods of
improving metaverse telepresence. We suggest looking into
further elements and tactics to boost telepresence, immer-
sion, and realism in order to support metaverse developers.
Furthermore, self-selection bias may be present because par-
ticipation of participants was optional. Consequently, to ver-
ify the generalizability of our results to diverse metaverse
scenarios, future research could expand the participant pool
to include a larger and more representative sample. We sug-
gest that in order to comprehend the metaverse phenomena
fully, future studies employ a triangulation strategy that
combines self-report data, in-depth interviews, and observa-
tional techniques.
Further investigation is also required to elucidate the
ways in which technical features impact telepresence, avatar
ownership, and control experiences, contributing to the
expanding body of knowledge in the metaverse and virtual
reality domains. Lastly, even though the bulk of research
focused on cognitive processes to understand conative
behavioral goals in the metaverse, the success of metaverse
applications in retail settings may be enhanced by including
customer emotional reactions, such as arousal. Positive
directions could be taken by future research by looking at
traits like engagement in the metaverse, individual innova-
tion, and risk perception.
